stem.text: Let \( f(x) = \frac{15 x}{\left(x^{2} + 6\right)^{2}} \) and \( a_n = f(n) \). State the conditions the integral test requires for the series \( \sum_{n=5}^{\infty} a_n \), and use the test to determine whether the series converges or diverges.

answer_key.label: \( \sum a_n \) converges, because f is positive, decreasing and continuous on \( [5, \infty) \) and \( \lim_{b\to\infty} \int_{5}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \frac{15}{62} \).

worked_solution.text: On \( [5, \infty) \), f is positive, continuous because \( \left(x^{2} + 6\right)^{2} \) is positive there, and decreasing because \( f^{\prime}(x) = - \frac{45 \left(x^{2} - 2\right)}{\left(x^{2} + 6\right)^{3}} \) is negative there.
An antiderivative of f is \( - \frac{15}{2 x^{2} + 12} \).

\( \lim_{b\to\infty} \left[- \frac{15}{2 x^{2} + 12}\right]_{5}^{b} = \lim_{b\to\infty} \left(- \frac{15}{2 b^{2} + 12} - \left(- \frac{15}{62}\right)\right) \), and the first term approaches \( 0 \), so \( \lim_{b\to\infty} \int_{5}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \frac{15}{62} \).
worked_solution.rule_named: limit notation on an improper integral

worked_solution.text: The integral converges, so by the integral test \( \sum_{n=5}^{\infty} a_n \) converges.

options.label: \( \sum a_n \) converges, because f is positive, decreasing and continuous on \( [5, \infty) \) and \( \lim_{b\to\infty} \int_{4}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \frac{15}{44} \).
options.derivation: the improper integral started at 4, an index the series does not use
